figures.alt: Illustrated cover for the article: the title 'From Fanum Fortunae to Palladio' above a drawing of the Vitruvian basilica in plan and perspective, with a ruined column in the foreground.
figures.caption: Cover image by the author.

figures.alt: Photograph of the excavation site of the Basilica of Fano in a town square, with exposed foundations and covered remains between modern arcaded buildings.
figures.caption: Fig. 1. The archaeological excavation complex of the Basilica of Fano as it appears today (photograph by the author).

figures.alt: Plan of the Basilica of Fano with its rectangular colonnade, next to a three-dimensional model of the building with a tiled roof.
figures.caption: Fig. 2. Plan of the Basilica of Fano and external volumetric elevation, as presented in the first reconstruction developed in the author’s doctoral dissertation (reconstruction by the author; 1997 doctoral dissertation, La Basilica di Fano di Vitruvio, dalla critica storiografica a nuovi rilievi e ipotesi di ricostruzione [The Basilica of Vitruvius in Fano: From historiographical criticism to new surveys and reconstruction hypotheses]).

figures.alt: Historic engraving with the plan of the Basilica of Fano above and its sectional elevation below, from a Renaissance edition of Vitruvius.
figures.caption: Fig. 3. Plan and sectional elevation of the Basilica of Fano in the reconstruction attributed to Andrea Palladio, in M. Vitruvius, I dieci libri dell’architettura [The Ten Books on Architecture], translated and annotated by Daniele Barbaro (Venice: Francesco de’ Franceschi Senese and Giovanni Chrieger, 1567), pp. 219–221. Source: e-rara / Stiftung Bibliothek Werner Oechslin, Public Domain.

figures.alt: Urban plan of the centre of Fano with the reconstructed forum and the proposed position of the Basilica of Vitruvius marked in red.
figures.caption: Fig. 4. Reconstruction of the Forum of Fanum Fortunae, proposing the location of the Basilica of Vitruvius in present-day Piazza Andrea Costa, 2013 drawing (drawing by the author).

figures.alt: Aerial view of the excavation area overlaid with the plan of the reconstructed basilica, with the matching remains marked in red.
figures.caption: Fig. 5. Overlay of the reconstruction of the Basilica of Vitruvius and the current state of the excavations. The correspondences identified to date are highlighted in red (reconstruction by the author, www.maindh.it).

figures.alt: Photograph of the excavated base of a large brick column and pilaster, with a measuring rod for scale.
figures.caption: Fig. 6. Remains of the large column and pilaster of the giant order of the Basilica of Fano, with sandstone masonry facing and an opus caementicium core (photograph by the author).

figures.alt: Two digital renderings of the interior of the reconstructed basilica, showing giant columns rising through two storeys with galleries.
figures.caption: Fig. 7. Interior views of the Basilica of Vitruvius, highlighting the giant order extending across both storeys, 2014 (reconstruction by the author, www.maindh.it).

figures.alt: Photograph of the courtyard of Villa Sarego with giant rusticated Ionic columns supporting two levels of loggias.
figures.caption: Fig. 8. Andrea Palladio, Villa Sarego, Santa Sofia di Pedemonte (San Pietro in Cariano, Verona), courtyard with the giant Ionic columns of rusticated stone. Photo: Hans A. Rosbach, 2011, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

figures.alt: Two photographs of the White House in Washington: the north front with its pedimented portico and the south front with its curved portico.
figures.caption: Fig. 9. The White House complex, designed by James Hoban in 1792 in the Neo-Palladian style. Public domain (work of the U.S. federal government), via Wikimedia Commons
